title: Secure Access and Software Supply Chain: IAP, Impersonation, WIF, Binary Authorization
bodyMarkdown:
## Remove bastions, public IPs, and long-lived keys

The legacy access pattern is a bastion host with a public IP, shared SSH keys, and service account key files in CI. Each is an attack surface and an audit gap. Google Cloud replaces them with three identity-based building blocks: **Identity-Aware Proxy** for human access, **service account impersonation** for just-in-time elevation, and **Workload Identity Federation** for workloads outside Google Cloud. A fourth, **Binary Authorization**, controls what is allowed to run.

## Pick the identity product first

Most identity mistakes start with a product chosen for the wrong population. The [identity products comparison](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/identity-products) separates them by who is authenticating.

| Who or what authenticates | Use | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Customers of your own app | **Identity Platform** (CIAM) | Email and password, Google, Facebook, Apple, phone, SAML and OIDC, SMS MFA, multi-tenancy |
| Your employees and groups as Google-managed accounts | **Cloud Identity** or Google Workspace | Central users and groups |
| Employees, partners and contractors from an external IdP, no account sync | **Workforce Identity Federation** | OIDC or SAML 2.0; pools at organization level |
| Workloads outside Google Cloud | **Workload Identity Federation** | Replaces service account keys |
| An application calling a Google API | **API key** | A standard key does not authenticate a principal; it ties requests to a project for billing and quota, so IAM cannot authorize it |
| What an authenticated principal may do | **IAM** | Authorization, not authentication |

**Identity Platform versus Firebase Authentication.** [Firebase Authentication](https://cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/product-comparison) uses Identity Platform as its backend and targets consumer apps with a subset of the features. Identity Platform adds OIDC and SAML sign-in, MFA, multi-tenancy, blocking functions, BAA coverage and a 99.95% SLA, and moving up needs no app changes. In the October 2026 docs the names are unchanged: Identity Platform is the Google Cloud product, and Firebase Authentication with Identity Platform is its upgraded Firebase form.

**Multi-tenancy.** A [tenant](https://cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/multi-tenancy) is a silo inside one project with its own user database, identity providers, IAM and audit settings, quota and usage metrics. A B2B SaaS gives each customer a tenant holding that customer's SAML or OIDC provider. Documented limits include no per-tenant blocking functions and no way to disable account linking.

**Altostrat Media.** Its staff, on Google Identity plus third-party IdPs, are workforce users: Cloud Identity or Workforce Identity Federation. Its subscribers signing up for a personalized app are customers: Identity Platform. An API key in the subscriber app would never tell the backend who the subscriber is.

## Identity-Aware Proxy

IAP is an application-level authorization layer: instead of relying on network firewalls, you authorize by identity and IAM role. Per the [IAP overview](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/concepts-overview), it protects apps on App Engine, Cloud Run, Compute Engine, GKE, and on-premises backends, and removes the need for a VPN or bastion.

**IAP for HTTPS applications.** The user is redirected to sign in, and IAP checks that they hold the **IAP-secured Web App User** role before forwarding the request. The documentation is explicit that direct access must be prevented: firewall off traffic that does not arrive through the load balancer, and for Cloud Run restrict ingress or disable the `run.app` URL. An IAP-protected app with a reachable public backend is not protected.

**IAP TCP forwarding for SSH and RDP.** The [TCP forwarding documentation](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/using-tcp-forwarding) lists the requirements for reaching VMs that have **no external IP**:

- A firewall rule allowing ingress from **35.235.240.0/20** (or `2600:2d00:1:7::/64` for IPv6) to the target ports.
- The `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` (IAP-secured Tunnel User) role, granted per VM or at project level.
- For SSH, the page lists `roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1`; for VMs that use OS Login it points to the OS Login role setup (below) instead of the metadata-editing permissions.
- Connect with `gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE --tunnel-through-iap`, the console SSH button (which routes through IAP when there is no external IP), IAP Desktop, or `gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel INSTANCE 3389` for RDP.

Conditions can narrow grants using CEL, for example restricting to `destination.port == 22`. Sessions disconnect after an hour of inactivity, bandwidth is throttled to prevent abuse, usage is audit-logged, and IAP TCP forwarding integrates with VPC Service Controls.

**Adding context.** Access levels from Access Context Manager (device posture, IP, geolocation) attach to IAP so access depends on more than identity; this is the Chrome Enterprise Premium pattern from module 3.

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| SSH or RDP to private VMs | IAP TCP forwarding |
| Internal web admin app, per-user authorization | IAP for HTTPS |
| Device-aware, VPN-less access | IAP plus access levels (Chrome Enterprise Premium) |
| Access to an on-prem app | IAP with an on-premises backend |

### OS Login on top of the tunnel

IAP controls who can reach the VM; [OS Login](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/oslogin/set-up-oslogin) controls who becomes which Linux user, driven by IAM.

| Role | Grants | Granted at |
|---|---|---|
| `roles/compute.osLogin` | Login without sudo | Project or instance |
| `roles/compute.osAdminLogin` | Login with sudo | Project or instance |
| `roles/compute.osLoginExternalUser` | Lets accounts from another organization configure POSIX information; added on top of a login role | Organization only, by an organization administrator |
| `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` | Required if the VM has an attached service account | That service account |
| `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` | The tunnel itself | VM or project |

- Setting `enable-oslogin` to TRUE in project or instance metadata **deletes the VM's `authorized_keys`** and stops accepting SSH keys stored in metadata. The `compute.requireOsLogin` organization policy rejects requests that set it to false.
- **2-step verification** is enforced only when **both** `enable-oslogin` and `enable-oslogin-2fa` are TRUE. Users without 2SV on their Google Account or domain are then denied, and it is not enforced for service-account users.
- For SSH from the console or gcloud, grant the OS Login roles at the project level, or add a role that contains `compute.projects.get`.
- Access follows IAM: changing a role changes access, and connections are audit-logged.
- **Expiring admin access:** Compute Engine accepts conditional bindings, so grant `roles/compute.osAdminLogin` with a `request.time` condition instead of a standing sudo grant, or use a PAM entitlement when each elevation should be requested and approved.

### IAP for external people: Workforce Identity Federation

When partner staff need an internal web app without a VPN or Google accounts, enable [IAP with Workforce Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/use-workforce-identity-federation): a workforce pool and provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID or any OIDC or SAML 2.0 IdP) in your organization, an OAuth client, then IAP-secured Web App User granted to workforce principals, optionally with IAM conditions.

- Grant to a **principal identifier**, such as `principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL/group/GROUP_ID`, never to an email address.
- Each IAP-enabled application accepts **one workforce pool with one provider**, so it cannot give every customer its own IdP; that is the Identity Platform tenant use case.
- It works on the resources IAP supports: App Engine, Compute Engine, Cloud Run and GKE.
- **Device-based access levels are not available.** Request-context access levels on IP address, and on time and date, still are. Programmatic access is supported only for Google service accounts.
- If users already live in an external authentication system and moving them to Google accounts is impractical, IAP can instead use Identity Platform external identities.

| Users reaching the app | Design |
|---|---|
| Employees with Google accounts | IAP with Google sign-in, plus access levels |
| Partner staff from their own IdP, no Google accounts | IAP with Workforce Identity Federation |
| Customers or subscribers | Identity Platform in the app, or IAP external identities |

## Service account impersonation

Impersonation lets an authenticated principal obtain a **short-lived token** for a service account and act as it. The [impersonation documentation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-impersonation) identifies `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` as the role containing the `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken` permission. Two properties make it the preferred pattern:

- **No key to leak.** There is nothing to download, store, or rotate.
- **Dual-identity audit trail.** Most audit logs record both the caller and the impersonated service account, whereas a downloaded key only ever shows the service account.

For on-call elevation, grant TokenCreator on the privileged service account, scoped with an IAM Condition, or wrap it in a Privileged Access Manager entitlement so the grant expires on its own. The engineer holds the permission only while needed and never possesses a credential file.

Service account keys remain the last resort. The [IAM best practices](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/using-iam-securely) say to avoid them when any alternative exists, and to rotate by creating a new key, switching apps, disabling the old key, then deleting it. Enforce the position with the `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` organization policy.

## Workload Identity Federation

WIF lets workloads outside Google Cloud call Google Cloud APIs **without service account keys**. The [WIF documentation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation) lists supported providers: AWS, Azure, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, on-premises Active Directory, GitHub, GitLab, any OIDC or SAML 2.0 provider, X.509 client certificates, Kubernetes clusters, and Terraform. The flow: the external workload presents its IdP token, Google Security Token Service validates it against a **workload identity pool provider**, applies **attribute mapping**, and returns a short-lived Google credential.

Key design facts:

- **Pool and provider:** a pool manages external identities; a provider describes the trust relationship with one IdP. Create **separate pools per environment** (dev, staging, prod).
- **Attribute mapping** (CEL): `google.subject` is required (max 127 characters); you can map up to 50 custom `attribute.NAME` values and optionally `google.groups`.
- **Attribute conditions** (CEL) accept or reject credentials, for example only a given repository and branch. They defend against the **confused deputy** problem.
- **Two access modes:** **direct resource access**, granting roles straight to the federated identity (recommended where the service supports it), or **impersonation**, where the identity gets `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on a service account.
- **Hardening:** never grant roles to *all* identities in a pool, use fully qualified resource names, and reference the project **number** rather than the ID.

**Rule of thumb:** before downloading a service account key, ask whether the workload is inside Google Cloud (use an attached service account or impersonation) or outside (use WIF).

| Workload location | Preferred credential |
|---|---|
| Compute Engine, Cloud Run, GKE | Attached service account / Workload Identity for GKE |
| Developer laptop | `gcloud auth application-default login` or impersonation |
| GitHub Actions, GitLab, AWS, Azure, on-prem | Workload Identity Federation |
| Human needing temporary elevation | Impersonation or PAM |

## Securing the software supply chain

Provenance and integrity of what you deploy matter as much as who can deploy.

### Artifact Analysis

The [Artifact Analysis documentation](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/artifact-analysis) describes software composition analysis and metadata storage. **Automatic scanning** triggers when an image is pushed to Artifact Registry, and vulnerability information keeps updating as new threats appear; it includes OS packages and application-language packages such as Go, Java, Python, and Node.js. **On-demand scanning** is run by command, can scan local images before pushing, and does not update data after the scan. Metadata is stored as **notes and occurrences**, which Binary Authorization can use in policy, and it supports **SBOM** generation and storage. Findings can surface in Security Command Center.

### Binary Authorization

The [Binary Authorization overview](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview) describes a deploy-time control with two modes: **enforce** (images that conform to policy are allowed, others blocked) and **monitor** via continuous validation (check-based platform policies, listed as Preview). Supported platforms are GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Service Mesh, and Google Distributed Cloud.

- **Policy** contains rules that state what an image must satisfy.
- **Attestors** verify **attestations**, digitally signed records that an image completed a prior stage such as build and vulnerability scan.
- **Break-glass** supports emergency deployments, and **dry-run** lets you test a policy without blocking.
- Cloud Build integration provides **provenance**, and decisions are logged in Cloud Audit Logs.

An image pulled onto a developer laptop and pushed manually has no attestation from the approved pipeline, so the policy blocks it. Attestors also map directly onto separation of duties: the group that controls the attestation key is distinct from the group that deploys.

## End-to-end flow

1. CI (GitHub Actions) authenticates through WIF with attribute conditions limiting repo and branch.
2. The pipeline builds the image, pushes it to Artifact Registry, and Artifact Analysis scans it.
3. If the scan passes, the pipeline creates a Binary Authorization attestation.
4. GKE or Cloud Run admits the workload only if the policy is satisfied.
5. Operators reach VMs and admin apps via IAP, and elevate via impersonation or PAM.

## Common mistakes and anti-patterns

- **Exporting a service account key "just for CI".** Use WIF; ban key creation by org policy.
- **Granting WIF access to the whole pool** or omitting attribute conditions, so any repository in the IdP tenant can authenticate.
- **One WIF pool for every environment.**
- **IAP with a reachable backend.** Anyone who finds the direct URL or IP bypasses it.
- **Opening port 22 to `0.0.0.0/0`** when the 35.235.240.0/20 IAP range is enough.
- **Binary Authorization without a signing step.** A policy that requires attestations with no pipeline creating them blocks everything; one with permissive rules blocks nothing. Start in dry-run.
- **Same group deploys and holds the attestation key**, which collapses separation of duties.
- **Treating vulnerability scanning as deployment control.** Scanning produces findings; only an enforcement point (Binary Authorization) blocks.
- **Granting TokenCreator unconditionally and permanently**, which is just a standing privileged role.
- **An API key as a user identity.** It identifies a project, not a person.
- **Workforce Identity Federation for your customers**, or Workload Identity Federation for people. Match the product to the population.
- **Setting only `enable-oslogin-2fa`.** Without `enable-oslogin` there is no enforcement and metadata keys still work.
- **`roles/compute.osLoginExternalUser` granted at project level.** It is granted at the organization only.
- **Promising device posture for partner staff behind IAP with Workforce Identity Federation.** Device-based access levels are unavailable there.

## Exam tips

- **Bastion and public IPs gone:** IAP TCP forwarding for SSH/RDP plus IAP for HTTPS apps, authorized by IAM; the firewall must allow 35.235.240.0/20.
- **IAP needs a closed back door:** block direct access to the backend or IAP can be bypassed.
- **No service account keys:** inside Google Cloud use attached service accounts or impersonation; outside use Workload Identity Federation.
- **Just-in-time elevation without a key:** grant `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` on the privileged service account, scoped by a condition or PAM.
- **GitHub Actions or other external CI:** WIF with an attribute condition and a separate pool per environment.
- **WIF access modes:** direct resource access is preferred where supported; otherwise `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on a service account.
- **Deploy-time supply-chain gate:** Binary Authorization with attestors, not vulnerability scanning alone; Artifact Analysis feeds the scan result.
- **Break-glass and dry-run** exist in Binary Authorization; use dry-run before enforcing.
- **Customers versus workforce:** your app's customers use Identity Platform (SAML, OIDC, MFA, multi-tenancy; Firebase Authentication lacks these); employees and partners use Cloud Identity or Workforce Identity Federation; API keys identify a project, and IAM only authorizes.
- **Per-customer enterprise SSO with isolated users:** Identity Platform tenants, one per customer.
- **Partner staff, no VPN, no Google accounts:** IAP plus Workforce Identity Federation, granted to principal identifiers; device-based access levels are not available, IP and time conditions are.
- **SSH hardening:** OS Login needs `enable-oslogin` and `enable-oslogin-2fa` both TRUE for 2-step verification, and enabling it deletes metadata keys; external-organization users also need `osLoginExternalUser` at the organization.
- **Expiring sudo:** `osAdminLogin` with a `request.time` condition or a PAM entitlement, not a standing grant.
